items.title: Young people lose hearing
items.text: The British Medical Journal published a study which showed that 1 billion young people were at risk of hearing loss. Researchers shared their analysis of data from 2000 to 2021 on unsafe listening practices. If the volume is too loud for too long, headphones, a concert, or even a restaurant could cause irreversible damage. Young people are complaining about persistent ringing in their ears, although their hearing tests look normal. However, several years later, their hearing reduces. The loud sounds damage sensory cells in the cochlea, the snail-looking part in the inner ear. Once these cells die, you can’t get them back. 85 decibels sound like a blender, 100 decibels sound like a subway train, and 120 decibels sound like a concert or a siren. According to experts, 85 decibels during a 40-hour work week is the maximum safe limit. Just 2.5 hours of 92 decibels can damage your ears. However, only one episode of intense noise exposure can lead to lifelong hearing loss. Difficult words: irreversible (impossible to change or return to a previous condition), persistent (continue over a long period of time), exposure (affected by something). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

items.title: Young people lose hearing
items.text: British scientists published a study about people 12 to 34 years old; the study said that more than 1 billion of them had hearing problems. Many young people complain about nonstop ringing in their ears. Hearing tests show no problems, but when doctors repeat the test some years later, the hearing is worse. The main reasons are headphones, concerts, and restaurants where the sounds are too loud for too long. The sound damages the cells in the inner ear, and once this damage happens, you cannot change it. Scientists say that the safe limit for our ears is 85 decibels over a 40-hour work week. 85 decibels are the sound of a blender , while 100 decibels are the sound of a train. We can also suddenly lose our hearing when we experience a very loud noise just once. Difficult words: cell (the smallest part in the human body), decibel (the unit which people use to measure loudness), blender (an electric mixing machine). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

items.title: Young people lose hearing
items.text: Experts say that more than 1 billion young people cannot hear well. They are between 12 and 34 years old. Young people often hear a loud continuous noise in their ears. Their hearing tests look normal. Later, their hearing test results are worse. Experts know reasons why this situation happens. Young people listen to their headphones . They go to concerts. The music is too loud. Sometimes, music in restaurants is loud, too. Decibels tell us how loud something is. The sound of a food mixer is 85 decibels. The sound of a train is 100 decibels. Experts say that it is safe to listen to 85 decibels at work. Sometimes we can lose hearing when we hear something very loud only once. Loud noise kills the cells in our ears. We cannot fix the situation. Difficult words: result (the information we get from a test or experiment), headphones (a device which people wear over their ears to listen to music), cell (the smallest part in the human body). items.title: Prince Harry speaks about social media
items.text: During a visit to the European Parliament in Brussels, Prince Harry delivered a powerful speech condemning social media platforms for exposing children to online harassment, bullying, and mental health risks. The Duke of Sussex described short-form content and platform algorithms as brainwashing on an extraordinary scale and advocated for stricter digital regulation. At the same time, he pointed out audience members who were scrolling on their phones during his address, and urged them to consider the real-world harm inflicted on vulnerable youth. Harry backed the proposed EU Kids Act, which aims to hold tech platforms accountable rather than placing the burden entirely on parents. Accompanied by Meghan Markle who attended briefly following recent difficult personal news the couple met with lawmakers and supported grieving families who lost children to online harm. EU leaders praised their advocacy, and promised to introduce strict age verification, restrict addictive features, and fine non-compliant platforms. Difficult words: condemn (to disapprove of something), inflict (to cause something unpleasant, harmful, or painful to be suffered by someone), non-compliant (failing or refusing to follow rules, or official regulations). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

items.title: Prince Harry speaks about social media
items.text: Prince Harry and Meghan Markle visited the European Parliament in Brussels to support new rules for protecting children online. Prince Harry spoke to EU politicians and warned that social media companies are hurting young people through addictive apps and online bullying . He pointed out that many people in the audience were checking their phones while he was speaking. Harry supported the new EU Kids Act, which wants social media companies to take responsibility for keeping kids safe online. Meghan joined Harry to view a memorial for young people who died because of online harm. She didn’t give a speech though. European leaders thanked them and promised to continue making internet rules safer for children. Difficult words: addictive (making you to want more of something or continue doing something), bullying (hurting someone again and again), memorial (an object, or event established to remember a person who died). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

items.title: Prince Harry speaks about social media
items.text: Prince Harry visited Brussels. He speaks in the European Parliament about children and online world. Harry says that social media apps are dangerous for children. They cause bad problems like bullying . He tells leaders that looking at phones all day is bad for kids. Some leaders are looking into their phones while he is speaking. Harry wants social media companies to follow strict rules to keep young people safe. Meghan comes with Harry. They meet families of children who die because of social media. EU leaders say that Harry is right. They want to make the internet safer for all children. Difficult words: dangerous (not safe), bullying (hurting someone again and again), because of (as a result of something). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

items.title: Grand Theft Auto 6 is released worldwide
items.text: Grand Theft Auto 6 (GTA 6) has finally been released. Millions of video game fans worldwide are now playing it. They have waited 13 years for a new GTA game since the release of GTA 5. Gaming experts say the latest version could be the biggest entertainment release in history. It has already sold millions of copies, and it is set to make billions of dollars. Some fans are so excited that they are taking days off work or school to play it. An HR company in the UK said that workers in Britain booked around 83,000 days off because of the game. Many fans tried to make their games consoles think they lived in New Zealand by changing their region settings. They tried this so they could play the game earlier. GTA 6 has received excellent reviews for its high-quality, realistic graphics and exciting story. Players get to explore a huge world of crime and follow the lives of two criminals. However, many experts warn that the game is unsuitable for children under the age of 17. That is because it contains violence, killing, car theft, bad language, drugs, alcohol and sexual content. Media expert Jasmine Hood Miller said: "In GTA, players commit crimes, sometimes against ordinary people who did nothing wrong." She added: "GTA is a very well-made game that teens find fun to play." items.title: Wire upgrade at fault for grounding all US flights
items.text: Thousands of flights across the USA were grounded on Friday the 13th following a major communications failure in the country's air traffic control system. The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) ordered a nationwide ground stop after problems with radar and communications equipment. More than 3,500 airplanes were in the air at the time. Thousands of flights were cancelled, leaving passengers stranded at airports nationwide. The problem was eventually traced to an overloaded router, possibly as a result of maintenance work to replace decades-old copper wires with fibre-optic cables. The FAA lifted the ground stop almost five hours later. Operations may take days to return to normal. The incident sparked widespread concern. Officials quickly reassured the public that it was not another 9/11. The US homeland security secretary said there had been no indication of a cyberattack or national security threat. He described the incident as a "telecommunications outage". Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy blamed the failure on outdated infrastructure. He said: "We have old switches and old routers. We use 1980s little copper lines." He added: "It's an old system that went down. It went down everywhere. It got overloaded." Duffy warned that systems would "continue to break" unless Congress allocated extra funds. He said: "I can't build things if I don't have money." items.title: France blames Iran for cyberattack on freezers
items.text: The French government has blamed Iran for a cyberattack on supermarket freezers and refrigerators across France. The attacks happened last month. They hit around 700 supermarkets and shops. Hackers took control of the cooling systems in the fridges and freezers. Temperatures increased to more than 50 degrees Celsius. Thousands of tons of frozen food melted. Stores had to throw the food away because it was no longer safe to eat. The French Foreign Minister said the attack was on a level never seen before. France believes an Iranian cyber unit carried out the attack. Iran has strongly denied it was involved in the attacks and blamed the French government for them. Security experts have warned that cyberattacks could be more dangerous in the future. Similar attacks have already affected other European countries. A French blood bank has also been hit. Fortunately, workers stopped the blood products from being damaged. Cybersecurity expert Gerome Billois stated: "At the moment, they are attacking easy equipment, but we should be prepared to see attacks on other systems like water or electricity." Weak computer security can let hackers attack places and services, such as hospitals, airports, public transport and banks. This can put people's lives in danger. items.title: Chef fired for refusing to put pineapple on pizza
items.text: An Italian chef in Brisbane, Australia, has been fired for refusing to put pineapple on pizzas, among other reasons. He went to the Fair Work Commission to fight his dismissal, but failed to get his job back. The chef stated that topping pizzas with the tropical fruit was an "insult to his culture". He claimed he was sacked from a restaurant in May after repeatedly refusing his boss's instructions to make pineapple and ham pizzas for diners. His employer contended that the refusal was one of several workplace issues. The commission rejected the chef's application because it was submitted after the deadline. The chef has since found a job at another Italian restaurant. The question of whether pineapple belongs on pizza is a controversial one. It continues to divide public opinion. Pizza purists are aghast at the idea, but it is an established menu staple in many countries. The Hawaiian pizza was reportedly invented in Canada in 1962 after a chef used ham and pineapple as toppings. The restaurant owner expressed his opinion on it. He admitted that while the pizza was not his "absolute favourite," he would not "turn his nose up at it". Many restaurateurs insist that customers should be free to enjoy whatever ingredients and toppings they choose. Although the Hawaiian pizza is popular internationally, many Italians regard it as "culinary heresy". Buy my 1,000 Ideas and Activities for Language Teachers eBook. items.title: Nvidia boss ends
items.text: Nvidia’s share price dropped sharply after its co-founder and longtime boss, Jensen Huang, suddenly resigned. His decision followed growing pressure and a company investigation into his secret relationship with a woman suspected of spying for China. Media reports also revealed a second affair with an executive inside Nvidia. To keep the business stable during this difficult change, the company appointed its finance chief as interim CEO to reassure investors and maintain stability during the unexpected leadership change. However, business experts warn that replacing Huang will be very hard, because he led Nvidia for 33 years and had no clear plan for a successor . Beyond problems inside the company, the scandal raises serious questions about whether Nvidia broke US rules by selling advanced computer chips to China. Experts expect US politicians and police to investigate the company closely. They warn that Nvidia’s weaker influence in Washington could lead to stricter trade limits and increase political tension between the US and China. Difficult words: executive (a person with senior managerial responsibility in a business organization), interim (temporary), successor (a person who takes over a job, office, or position after someone else leaves). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

items.title: Nvidia boss ends
items.text: Nvidia’s share price dropped quickly after its CEO and co-founder, Jensen Huang, suddenly resigned. He left the company after facing serious investigations over a personal affair with a woman who was a suspected Chinese spy , as well as a second affair with a company manager. To keep business running smoothly, Nvidia named its finance boss as temporary leader. Experts say replacing Huang will be very difficult because he led the company for 33 years and was very important to its success in AI. US officials plan to investigate what the company knew about the spying and whether Nvidia broke rules by selling computer chips to China. This problem could lead to stricter US trade laws and increased tension between America and China. Difficult words: spy (a person secretly collecting and reporting sensitive information for a foreign government or competitor), temporary (when something lasts for only some time), tension (a state of difficult relations between countries or people). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

items.title: Nvidia boss ends
items.text: Nvidia is a big tech company. Its boss, Jensen Huang, leaves his job suddenly . The company’s stock price falls. Huang leaves after news about his relationship with a woman who may be a spy for China. Nvidia chooses another boss for some time. So the business stays safe. Experts say that it will be very hard to find a new leader. Huang is the boss for 33 years. Now, US officials want to check if Nvidia breaks any rules. The company sells computer parts to China. This big problem may make trade between the US and China more difficult. Difficult words: suddenly (quickly, without a plan), stock price (how much one part of a company costs), spy (a person who gets information about other people or countries and they do not know about it). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

items.title: Microsoft stops on Friday the 13th
items.text: A major global Microsoft outage on Friday the 13th disrupted essential services for hundreds of thousands of users worldwide and affected Outlook, Teams, Microsoft 365, OneDrive, and Copilot. At the peak of the disruption, a monitoring website recorded over 130,000 reports for Outlook and 46,000 for Microsoft 365. Microsoft said a core process on its servers became overwhelmed and stopped responding, but ruled out a cyberattack and began a gradual recovery. A cybersecurity expert noted that the incident highlights the serious risks of businesses relying on a single technology provider for daily operations. When major cloud platforms fail, companies can lose access to emails, online meetings, and security verification codes, which brings daily work to a standstill . Experts advise organizations not to put all their eggs in one basket, and urge them to diversify their digital providers and prepare strong backup plans to stay resilient during future technical crashes. Difficult words: rule out (to eliminate or exclude something as a possibility or cause), standstill (a situation in which all movement, activity, or work has stopped completely), resilient (able to withstand or recover quickly from difficult conditions, shocks, or system failures). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

items.title: Microsoft stops on Friday the 13th
items.text: A huge Microsoft system failure on Friday the 13th stopped important services like Outlook, Teams, and Microsoft 365 from working around the world. More than 130,000 people reported problems with Outlook, and thousands couldn’t send emails or join online meetings. Microsoft said its computer servers got overloaded and stopped responding, though it confirmed this was not a cyberattack. The company slowly started fixing the problem to bring services back online. A technology expert explained that this crash shows the danger of businesses depending on just one tech company for all their daily work. He advised companies to use more than one provider and build strong backup plans so that one computer crash doesn’t stop their whole business from operating. Difficult words: failure (when something stops working properly), overloaded (given too much work, data, or weight to handle properly), failure (when something stops working properly). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

items.title: Microsoft stops on Friday the 13th
items.text: A big computer problem at Microsoft stops many services around the world on Friday. People cannot use Outlook email, Teams, or other work apps for hours. Microsoft says that its main computers have too much work. They stop working. But it is not an attack by hackers. The company starts slowly fixing the problem. Technology experts say that companies should not use only one big tech company for everything. If one system breaks, people cannot do their jobs. Businesses need good backup plans so they can keep working when a problem comes. Difficult words: main (the biggest or most important thing), fix (to repair), backup (an extra copy of data or a plan for a situation when something stops working). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

items.title: Man completes 28-year walk around the world
items.text: A British man has completed an amazing 28-year walk around the world. Former soldier Karl Bushby, 57, arrived home in the city of Hull in England on Monday. He started his adventure in November 1998 in Chile, South America. His plan was to walk all the way home without using cars, boats, buses, trains, or airplanes. During his journey, he travelled about 58,000 kilometres through 29 countries. He crossed frozen seas, deserts, mountains, and jungles. He also faced many dangers. These included encountering polar bears and kidnappers, and spending time in a Russian prison. His journey was expected to take 12 years. However, problems with money, visas, and borders made his trip a lot longer. Thousands of people welcomed Mr Bushby home. He was very happy to finally finish his journey. His mother was waiting outside his childhood home to greet him. Bushby joked: "Sorry to keep you waiting." He also told the cheering crowd that many people around the world had helped him get home. He said he could not have done it alone. Britain's Prime Minister congratulated him on his achievement. He praised Bushby's determination and belief in himself. Bushby told the Guardian newspaper that he wasn't so interested in walking. He said: "It's boring as hell." That didn't stop him walking across four continents. items.title: Women pay to break things
items.text: Across the UK, a growing number of people, especially women, are turning to so-called rage rooms to destroy everyday items like flat-screen televisions and crockery with mallets and hammers. Owners report that up to three-quarters of their customers are female. Many use the sessions to cope with everyday stress, child-rearing pressures, or deep emotional trauma such as bereavement . Psychologists note that societal expectations often force women to suppress anger, unlike sports events where men are traditionally permitted to shout freely. Inside a rage room, participants find a safe, controlled environment where they can express frustration without judgment . While smashing objects provides an immediate surge of adrenaline and physical relief, experts caution that it doesn’t serve as a permanent therapeutic cure for long-term psychological problems. Instead, they view it as a helpful short-term release of energy, and advise individuals dealing with deep-seated emotional pain to seek professional long-term support. Difficult words: bereavement (suffering the loss of a loved one through death), suppress (to forcibly hold back, control, or prevent the expression of a feeling), judgment (an opinion or decision formed after thought or legal process).
